title: The Line Nobody Ran: Coverage as a Floor, Not a Score

questions.question: A program calls five functions and asserts nothing at all. One of them has a deliberate defect. What does gcov report?
options: 100 percent of 5 lines, 0 never run, and the defect survives untouched
Zero percent, because no assertions ran
100 percent, but it flags the function whose result was discarded
It refuses to report on a program with no assertions
questions.explanation: Coverage answers one question: did this line run. It does not ask whether anything checked the result. A line that never ran certainly is not tested; a line that ran may or may not be.

questions.question: In a .gcov file, which count fields mean the line is code that never ran?
options: Both ##### and =====; the second means the block holding the line was never entered
Only #####; ===== marks a line that is not code
##### and -, since a dash means no count was recorded
Only =====; ##### marks a compiler-generated line
questions.explanation: Counting only ##### reported 5 never-run lines on a real file where the answer was 7. Both markers mean not covered.

questions.question: After counting both never-run markers, a hand count still said 56 executable lines where gcov said 64. What was missing?
options: The digits* form, which is code that ran but not in every instance, and is still code
The header lines numbered 0, which are executable
Lines marked with a dash, which gcov counts as executable
Blank lines, which gcov counts but the hand count skipped
questions.explanation: digits* appears with templates and inlining. Leaving it out of the executable count gave 87.50 percent instead of 89.06. Two of the three wrong attempts were wrong in the flattering direction.

questions.question: Why does percent_covered return 100 for a file with no executable lines, and what should a caller do about it?
options: It is true and useless, so print the executable count beside the percentage: 100 percent of 0 and of 600 are the same number and not the same claim
It should return 0, since nothing was tested
It should return an error, since the file was not parsed
Nothing; a file with no code needs no coverage so the number is correct and sufficient
questions.explanation: The parser keeps ok separate from the counts for the same reason: valid output about a file with no code is a different fact from text that was never a gcov report, and confusing them would report perfect coverage of a file it failed to read.

questions.question: On a line of the form return a && b, exercised with one input, gcov reported three numbers. Which is the one most often quoted, and which is the most informative?
options: Lines executed 100 percent is quoted; taken at least once 50 percent is informative, since half the branch outcomes never happened
Branches executed 100 percent is quoted; lines executed is informative
All three agreed at 100 percent, so the question does not arise
Taken at least once is quoted; it is also the least informative
questions.explanation: Lines executed 100 percent of 2, branches executed 100 percent of 6, taken at least once 50 percent of 6. Branches executed only means the branch instruction ran; taken at least once means both outcomes occurred.

questions.question: Which of these can coverage never report on, even in principle?
options: The line that should exist and does not: a missing bounds check or timeout has no line to be uncovered
A line in a header that was included but never compiled
A line executed only in a release build
A line inside a template that was never instantiated
questions.explanation: That is the largest blind spot and the one with no tool in it. Coverage can only report on code that was written, which is why a review and a specification sit at the bottom of the instrument list with nothing automated beneath them.
